Join us and together, we'll build a tool that empowers farmers and showcases innovation with real impact.
summary: GroundTruth is a decentralised, data-driven agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make better crop-rotation decisions and improve soil health in a changing climate. It combines NASA POWER satellite-based climate observations with locally collected rainfall and temperature readings submitted by community volunteers. Using Chainlink's Decentralised Oracle Network (DON) and Runtime Environment (CRE), the platform validates these observations through digital signatures, peer agreement, and comparison with NASA data, producing locally adjusted climate information. Farmers can then explore ranked crop rotations from FAO EcoCrop database based on their location, soil characteristics, and farming priorities, with explanations behind each recommendation. GroundTruth also introduces a sustainable incentive model in which farmer subscriptions fund volunteer rewards through a fully backed reward mechanism. By connecting satellite intelligence, community participation, blockchain-based verification, and agricultural decision support, GroundTruth aims to bridge the gap between regional climate data and real field conditions.
details:
GroundTruth – Detailed Project Summary

1. What the Project Does and How It Works

GroundTruth is an agricultural decision-support platform designed to help farmers make better-informed crop-rotation decisions using climate information that reflects local field conditions. It addresses a key limitation of satellite-based climate data: NASA POWER provides valuable regional observations, but its grid cells cover tens of kilometres, meaning rainfall and temperature in a particular village or field can differ from the regional average.

GroundTruth combines NASA POWER climate data with local rainfall and temperature measurements submitted by community volunteers. The process begins when volunteers record their daily observations and sign them digitally using their blockchain wallets. The backend verifies these signatures, stores the readings and commits a cryptographic hash of the daily collection to the blockchain. This creates a tamper-evident record of the data before it is processed.

The next stage is designed around Chainlink's Runtime Environment (CRE) and Decentralised Oracle Network (DON). Oracle nodes independently retrieve the committed readings and corresponding NASA data, then apply the same deterministic validation rules. These checks are designed to identify forged submissions, readings that are implausible compared with NASA's data, and measurements that significantly disagree with other local observations. A minimum quorum of three agreeing readings is required, and corrections are reduced when there is insufficient supporting data.

When the oracle nodes reach agreement, a signed report is sent to the FieldOracle smart contract. The contract checks the report against the original data commitment, stores the resulting local climate corrections and reserves funds for volunteer rewards. Eligible volunteers can claim rewards using Merkle proofs.

Farmers can then select their location, provide soil information and choose their farming priorities. GroundTruth combines the NASA climate baseline with accepted local corrections to rank suitable crop-rotation options from FAO EcoCrop database, and explain the reasons behind its recommendations. Where local observations are unavailable, the application can still provide NASA-based guidance.

2. Benefits of the Project

GroundTruth offers several benefits to farmers and agricultural communities:

  • More locally relevant climate information: Combining regional satellite observations with community measurements helps account for differences between a regional climate average and actual field conditions.
  • Better-informed crop-rotation decisions: Farmers can compare ranked crop rotations using location, soil characteristics and their own priorities.
  • Greater transparency: The system is designed to make data submissions, verification results, climate corrections and reward allocations independently checkable.
  • Community participation: Local volunteers become active contributors to agricultural information rather than passive recipients of climate services.
  • Incentives for data collection: A proposed subscription model allocates 70% of farmer subscription payments to volunteer rewards and 30% to platform operations.
  • Explainable recommendations: Rather than presenting unexplained crop rankings, the decision engine is designed to show why particular rotations receive higher rankings.

3. Intended Impact

The long-term goal of GroundTruth is to help close the gap between regional climate information and the conditions farmers actually experience. By making local observations more useful and verifiable, the project aims to support agricultural decisions that are better adapted to local climate conditions.

It also aims to create a community-supported data network in which farmers benefit from improved information while volunteers receive incentives for contributing useful observations. This could encourage stronger local participation in climate monitoring and help build a more reliable information foundation for climate-aware agriculture.

Ultimately, GroundTruth seeks to contribute to improved soil-health management, more informed crop planning and greater resilience to changing climate conditions. These are intended impacts; the current prototype has not yet demonstrated measurable improvements in crop yields or field-level agricultural outcomes.

4. Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware and Software

GroundTruth was developed using a combination of web technologies, blockchain infrastructure, oracle tooling and NASA Earth observation data.

Data and external services

  • NASA POWER: Provides regional meteorological and long-term climate information used as the baseline for agricultural recommendations and as a reference for checking volunteer observations.
  • Chainlink Runtime Environment (CRE): Provides the framework for the decentralised oracle workflow.
  • Chainlink Decentralised Oracle Network (DON): The intended infrastructure for independent data processing and consensus.

Programming languages and development frameworks

  • Solidity: Used to develop the smart contracts responsible for subscriptions, reward tokens, data verification and reward settlement.
  • TypeScript: Used for the oracle workflow and associated off-chain logic.
  • Node.js: Used in the backend and JavaScript/TypeScript development environment.
  • React: Used to build the web application interface.
  • Vite: Used for the frontend development and production build process.

Blockchain and supporting tools

  • Foundry: Used to compile, deploy and test Solidity smart contracts.
  • Anvil: Used as the local blockchain environment for integration and end-to-end testing.
  • OpenZeppelin Contracts: Used for established smart-contract components.
  • viem: Used for blockchain interactions and contract integration.
  • Chainlink CRE SDK: Used to develop and type-check the oracle workflow.

Hardware

No custom electronic hardware was developed for the prototype. The intended volunteer measurement process uses basic field instruments, particularly rain gauges and thermometers, alongside an internet-connected device for submitting readings. The farmer and volunteer interfaces are delivered through a web application.

5. What Makes the Project Creative and Innovative?

The main innovation in GroundTruth is that it does not simply use satellite data to generate agricultural recommendations. It improves the local relevance of the information feeding those recommendations by introducing a community-powered and verifiable measurement system.

Its creativity lies in bringing together four elements that are often treated separately: NASA Earth observations, community-collected field measurements, decentralised verification and agricultural decision support.

The blockchain component has a practical purpose beyond token creation. It provides a public commitment to the submitted data, a verifiable record of processing and a programmable system for distributing rewards. Chainlink's oracle infrastructure is designed to reduce dependence on a single server for deciding which observations are accepted.

The reward mechanism is another distinctive element. By connecting farmer subscriptions to volunteer compensation, GroundTruth proposes an economic incentive for maintaining the local observation network. Merkle proofs also allow individual volunteers to claim rewards without requiring a separate on-chain transaction for every contributor during settlement.

Most importantly, the project focuses on improving the quality and trustworthiness of the information used for recommendations, rather than simply building another crop-selection application.

6. Factors Considered During Development

Several important factors influenced the design of GroundTruth:

  • Accuracy and geographical variation: NASA data is useful for regional climate analysis, but local rainfall and temperature differences must be considered.
  • Data integrity and manipulation: Wallet signatures, cryptographic batch commitments, peer agreement, plausibility checks and minimum reading thresholds were included to reduce fraudulent or unreliable submissions.
  • Transparency and accountability: Blockchain records and deterministic validation rules make the intended data-processing and reward process easier to inspect.
  • Reliability when data is limited: Corrections are designed to move closer to zero when there are too few supporting observations, reducing the influence of isolated readings.
  • Financial sustainability: The 70/30 subscription allocation was designed to support volunteer incentives while covering platform operations.
  • Scalability: Daily batch commitments and Merkle-based reward claims reduce the number of individual on-chain operations required as participation grows.
  • Usability and explainability: Farmers should be able to select their area, enter soil information, compare recommendations and understand why an option is ranked highly.
  • Agricultural limitations: The current recommendation model is deliberately a screening tool. It uses simplified seasonal climate and soil information rather than accounting for every factor affecting farm productivity.

7. Current Development Status

GroundTruth has been implemented as a working testnet prototype. Its clean-build verification recorded 90 passing automated tests across the smart contracts, oracle logic, backend and application. A further 22 end-to-end checks passed using a local Anvil blockchain, real contract deployments and backend integrations.

However, the project is not yet production-ready. The CRE workflow and live DON consensus were not run in the development environment. Live NASA data fetching, real-world wallet flows, agronomic accuracy, reward sizing, location verification, resistance to Sybil attacks and an independent security audit still require validation. The current crop-suitability data is illustrative and uses FAO EcoCrop database, but should be cross-checked with other validated agronomic data before real-world use.

GroundTruth is therefore a tested technical prototype with a clear path towards supervised field trials, rather than a fully validated agricultural service.
